items.prose: At Thursday's close a rule decides to sell 500 shares. Friday opens at £48.30 and closes at £48.90.
items.question: How much cash does the sale bring in, before costs, in £?

feedback.correct: The sale fills at Friday's open.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which price is the first after Thursday's close?

byKey.close: You filled at Friday's close. The order fills at the first price after it exists, Friday's open.

explain.text: Thursday's order trades at Friday's open, £48.30, so it brings in £24,150. Friday's close comes after the fill.

items.prose: A buy of 800 shares at £60.00. Commission £0.005 a share, minimum £1; half spread 3 bp.
items.question: What does the fill cost, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Commission per share, then 3 bp of the traded value.

byKey.full: You charged 6 bp, the whole spread. One fill crosses half of it.
byKey.min: You charged the £1 minimum, but $800 \times 0.005 = £4$ is above it.

explain.text: Commission is $800 \times 0.005 = £4$. The traded value is £48,000 and 3 bp of it is £14.40.

items.prose: An order of 50,000 shares in a share that trades 1,000,000 a day. Daily volatility is 2% and $c = 1$.
items.question: What impact does the square-root model give, in bp?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $Q/V = 0.05$; use its square root.

byKey.linear: You used $Q/V$ without the square root.

items.prose: An engine fills at the next open and returns targets, shares, cash and equity. Its signal secretly uses `close.shift(-1)`. A colleague's check compares only the equity of the cut run with the full run.
items.question: Why does their check miss the leak?

options.text: The leaky target on the last row before the cut fills after the cut.
The leak is too small to move equity.
options.why: You judged it by size. A `shift(-1)` signal is a huge leak; it reaches equity one row later.

options.text: Equity is noisy, so differences hide.
options.why: You blamed noise. The runs are deterministic; any change would show to 1e-9.

feedback.correct: So the check compares every column, targets included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. On which row does a target become shares?

explain.text: A target decided on row $c - 1$ becomes shares on row $c$, outside the comparison. Only the target column differs before the cut.

items.prose: A slow rule keeps the same target on 200 of its 250 days.
items.question: What do those 200 unchanged days cost in commission under our tariff (minimum £1)?

widget.label: Commission on unchanged days
widget.accept: £0: an order of 0 shares is never sent.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What order does an unchanged target make?

byKey.min: You charged the minimum on days with no order. Nothing is sent, so nothing is charged.

explain.text: An unchanged target gives an order of 0. `trade_cost(0, p)` is 0, so the minimum never applies.

items.prose: A sale of 250,000 shares arrives on a day that trades 1,500,000. The engine caps fills at 10% of the day's volume.
items.question: How many shares are still to sell after today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The cap is 10% of 1,500,000.

byKey.none: You filled the whole sale; the cap stops at 150,000.

explain.text: The cap is 150,000 shares. The rest, 100,000, waits for the next bar and its own volume.

items.prose: A rule made £120,000 gross over five years, paid £20,000 commission and traded £400m of shares.
items.question: At what half spread, in bp, does it break even?

feedback.correct: 2.5 bp of edge per £ traded, after commission.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take off the commission, then divide by the traded value.

byKey.no-comm: You left the commission in. It is paid whatever the spread.

explain.text: After commission the rule kept £100,000 on £400m traded, 0.00025 of it, which is 2.5 bp. A wider half spread makes it lose.

items.question: Which bugs does the look-ahead check catch? Select all that apply.

options.text: Positions scaled by `close.pct_change().std()` over the whole series
A signal from a centred rolling mean
Costs added to cash instead of taken off
options.why: You treated a cost bug as look-ahead. It reads no later rows, so cutting the data changes nothing.

options.text: Fills at the close of the signal bar
options.why: You treated an optimistic fill as look-ahead. It reads only row $t$; l5's fill rule guards against it.

feedback.correct: The check catches reads of later rows, and nothing else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which bugs read rows after $t$?

explain.text: A full-sample vol and a centred window both read rows after $t$, so a cut changes earlier rows. The other two read nothing later; they need their own tests.

items.prose: On `make_bars()`, `signal.shift(1) * r` gives a Sharpe of 0.82 and `signal * r` gives 20.38. The engine, filling at the next open, gives 0.57 for the same rule.
items.question: Why is the next-open figure lower than 0.82?

options.text: Half of each day's move happens overnight, and a next-open fill pays it instead of earning it.

options.why: You blamed costs. These figures are all before costs.

options.text: The engine still leaks a little.
options.why: You suspected a leak. The next-open fill is the most honest of the three; it is lower because it trades later.

feedback.correct: Trading later gives up the part of the move that has already happened.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What happens between the close and the next open?

explain.text: In `make_bars()` half of each move is overnight. By the open the price has moved towards the next close, so the fill gives up that part: 0.82 falls to 0.57.
